key_insight: Patient-level splits prevent subject leakage but cannot rule out acquisition confounders that predict diagnosis across the entire dataset.
clinical_relevance: Strong medical imaging benchmark performance may reflect acquisition patterns rather than pathology, limiting confidence in clinical generalization.
method: Audit whether a candidate confounder predicts diagnosis and can be decoded from images.
Test whether diagnostic scores depend on it and whether images add predictive value beyond it.
Measure discrimination after controlling for the confounder.
evidence_signal: In 236 DMR-IR patients evaluated with patient-disjoint splits, acquisition date predicted malignancy at AUROC 0.980 versus 0.949 for the best imaging arm; no imaging arm improved on date alone in paired-fold comparisons.
watch_item: Only eight cross-label same-date pairs from ten patients were available, preventing reliable assessment of pathology-specific discrimination within acquisition-date groups.
paper_title: Leakage-Free Is Not Confounder-Free: What a Patient-Level Split Cannot Certify About a Medical Imaging Benchmark
